proxytop|ProxyTop|1.annotation: The `exotic` example inspects an index to choose a different body in the `Index.Top` and `Index.Pop` cases. Frohlich, Foster, Kavvos and Wang give the host function a marker with only the `ProxyTop.PTop` constructor, so there is no older-variable case on which it can branch.

proxytop-only-top|ProxyTop|1.annotation: In a two-binder context $[a,b]$, a marker for the new variable has type `ProxyTop (Ctx.Empty :/: a :/: b) b`. The marker for the earlier variable keeps its original context $[a]$. To use it under the second binder, the construction needs a `ReifyIndex` instance that turns the saved marker into an index in the larger context.

contextual-embedding|STLCCtx|1.annotation: For $\lambda x.\lambda y.x$, the host binder names $x$ while its marker keeps the context at the first lambda. The occurrence beneath the second lambda needs one extension instance. Unembedding will read that instance to recover the single `Index.Pop` in the first-order `tt` example.

unembed|unembed|1.annotation: Both sides of the `unembed` signature in Figure 2 use the same `ts` and `t`. For instance, an open contextual term can be translated without assigning values to its free variables. The types ensure this preservation even for a custom reification instance. Recovering that same instance on a round trip requires more.

contextualise|contextualise|1.annotation: This translation builds the contextual representation of each term while retaining its original context and guest type. On variables it reconstructs the data for the binding site from the index. The reverse variable round trip (`indexIsoR`) asks whether that reconstruction recovers an arbitrary original instance.

proven|isoR|2.annotation: This direction starts with an arbitrary contextual term, which can already contain a reification instance. The authors' Lean proof uses `closedWorld` (every supplied reification instance must be reflexive or a recursive extension) to ensure reconstruction from an index recovers that stored instance. Together with `isoL` it supplies the isomorphism under that assumption.

core|indexIsoL|1.annotation: Starting with a typed position makes the induction straightforward: each `Index.Pop` becomes one stored extension, which in turn reifies to one `Index.Pop`. The first-order round-trip proof (`isoL`) uses this equality at every variable leaf.

indexIsoL|indexIsoL|1.annotation: The function `fromIndex` returns a variable package (`Var` in the paper), so the statement extracts its stored instance as field `.2` and its marker as field `.3`. Reifying with precisely that instance returns the original index. Field `.1` is the hidden binding context shared by the other two.

indexIsoL-proof|indexIsoL|1.annotation: In the `Index.Top` branch the two sides reduce to the same index. In the `Index.Pop` branch unfolding `fromIndex` and `weakenPVar` (`weakenCVar` in the paper) leaves a pop on each side. The induction hypothesis supplies equality of the indices inside those pops.

provability-closed-world|isoR|2.annotation: Suppose a theorem starts with a contextual term $e$. A proof about its rebuilt form yields a proof about $e$ by rewriting with `isoR`, which uses `closedWorld` (the restriction to the two defined reification instance forms). This lets the metatheoretic proof use induction on first-order syntax and return to the contextual statement.
